evergreen_facts.text: Stockholm is built on 14 islands where Lake Mälaren flows into the Baltic Sea.
The Stockholm archipelago stretches out from the city into the Baltic, with tens of thousands of islands.
Stockholm first appears in written records around 1252, and its founding is traditionally credited to Birger Jarl.
In the Stockholm Bloodbath of 1520, Danish king Christian II had scores of Swedish nobles and clergy executed.
Gamla stan, Stockholm's old town, dates from the 13th century and is a maze of narrow medieval streets.
The warship Vasa sank in Stockholm's harbour on her maiden voyage in 1628 and was raised largely intact in 1961.
Stockholm City Hall, completed in 1923, hosts the Nobel Prize banquet every December.
Drottningholm Palace near Stockholm, the Swedish royal family's home, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Every Nobel Prize except the Peace Prize is presented in Stockholm on 10 December, the date Alfred Nobel died.
Alfred Nobel, the chemist who invented dynamite and founded the Nobel Prizes, was born in Stockholm in 1833.
Skansen, opened on Stockholm's Djurgården island in 1891, was the world's first open-air museum.
Swedes around Stockholm celebrate Midsummer with flower crowns, dancing around a maypole and pickled herring.
Fika, a coffee break shared with friends or colleagues, often with a cinnamon bun, is a cherished Swedish custom.
Swedish meatballs are traditionally served with lingonberry jam, cream gravy and boiled or mashed potatoes.
Stockholm's Royal National City Park, created in 1995, was the world's first legally protected national urban park.
Stockholm hosted the 1912 Summer Olympics, and its purpose-built Olympic Stadium is still in use today.
